# Interfacial Octahedral Rotation Mismatch Control of

the Symmetry and Properties of SrRuO3

Epitaxial strain can be used to tune the properties of complex oxides with perovskite

structure. Beyond just lattice mismatch, the use of octahedral rotation mismatch at

heterointerfaces could also provide a route to manipulate material properties. Here, we

examine the evolution of the lattice (i.e., parameters, symmetry, and octahedral rotations) of

SrRuO3 films grown on substrates engineered to have the same lattice parameters, but


<!-- Page 2 -->


2

different octahedral rotations. SrRuO3 films grown on SrTiO3 (001) (no octahedral

rotations) and GdScO3-buffered SrTiO3 (001) (with octahedral rotations) substrates are

found to exhibit monoclinic and tetragonal symmetry, respectively. Electrical transport and

magnetic measurements reveal that the tetragonal films exhibit higher resistivity, lower

magnetic Curie temperatures, and more isotropic magnetism as compared to those with

monoclinic structure. Synchrotron-based half-order Bragg peak analysis reveals that the

octahedral rotation pattern in both film variants is the same (albeit with slightly different

magnitudes of in-plane rotation angles). The abnormal rotation pattern observed in

tetragonal SrRuO3 indicates a possible decoupling between the internal octahedral rotation

and lattice symmetry, which could provide new opportunities to engineer thin-film

structure and properties.

Keywords: SrRuO3; epitaxial strain; octahedral rotation; interfacial engineering; crystal symmetry

Perovskite oxides (with ABO3 chemistry) exhibit a diverse range of functional properties

which can be readily manipulated thus making such materials candidates for a wide range of

applications including logic,1,2 memories,3 sensing,4 photovoltaics,5 and more. The tunable nature

of such materials arises from the strong coupling between charge, orbital, spin, and lattice degrees

of freedom present in these systems whereby impacting one or more of these parameters can

result in dramatic changes to the properties. In films of such materials the use of epitaxial strain

enables direct manipulation of the lattice degree of freedom and subsequent control of charge,

orbital, and spin physics.6-8 Taking the canonical perovskite itinerant ferromagnetic SrRuO3 as an

example,9 ferromagnetism can be quenched under application of epitaxial strain due to a

suppression of the octahedral rotations that fundamentally changes the density of states of spin-up


<!-- Page 3 -->


3

and -down electrons at the Fermi level.10-12 In turn, SrRuO3, which exhibits orthorhombic

symmetry in the bulk, can be driven, under relatively large tensile or compressive strains, to

exhibit tetragonal symmetry.13, 14

In addition to epitaxial strain induced by lattice mismatch at heterointerfaces in

perovskite-perovskite heterostructures, an alternative interfacial coupling effect can also take

place when there exists an octahedral rotation mismatch between substrate and film.15-17 Due to

differences in the ionic radii of the A- and B-cations and oxygen and the semi-rigidity of the

oxygen octahedra cage, some perovskites exhibit octahedral rotations which can be described as a

combination of rotations along three orthogonal axes ([100], [010], and [001] in the pseudocubic

unit cell) with angles α, β, and γ (Figure 1a).18-20 Using Glazer notations, the relative magnitude

of the rotation along the three axes are denoted as a, b, and c, superscripted by 0, +, or – to

indicate no rotation, in-phase rotation, or out-of-phase rotation, respectively.18 Such octahedral

rotations lower the symmetry of the unit cell from cubic to orthorhombic, monoclinic,

rhombohedral, or triclinic. In turn, when a material with robust octahedral rotations is intimately

coupled with a material that exhibits no or lesser octahedral rotations, the mismatch of atomic

displacement at the heterointerface is generally accommodated by either deforming or rotating

the oxygen octahedra in the film.15, 17 In other words, this can be thought of as a propagation of

the octahedral rotation pattern from the substrate into the heteroepitaxial film.

Despite the potential for these different modes of heterointerfacial coupling, the pervasive

approach in the study of epitaxial strain has been to consider only the role of lattice mismatch-

induced strain (which is easily calculated and probed experimentally) while neglecting or

downplaying the role of octahedral rotation mismatch (which is hard to quantify and investigate).

In fact, only in recent years have researchers started to probe the effects of such octahedral

rotation mismatch effects in systems such as BiFeO3/La0.7Sr0.3MnO3,21 LaAlO3/SrTiO3,22


<!-- Page 4 -->


4

SrRuO3/substrates,23 and (LaNiO3)n/(SrMnO3)m superlattices24 using state-of-the-art transmission

electron microscopy and synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction. Despite these studies, a complete

physical picture of such interactions and understanding of the length scales over which such

effects can extend are still being developed. Nonetheless, it is becoming clear that in order to

exert complete, deterministic control of such heterostructures, knowledge of both the lattice and

octahedral rotation mismatch effects are needed. This is particularly important when one

considers that at room temperature nearly all commercially-available substrates used for

perovskite epitaxy (with the exception of cubic (a0a0a0) SrTiO3 and (LaAlO3)0.3(Sr2AlTaO6)0.7)25,

26 possess orthorhombic (a-a-c+) or rhombohedral (a-a-a-) symmetry with robust octahedral

rotations (this includes most rare earth scandate, aluminate, and gallate substrates).27, 28 Thus,

when researchers switch between substrates with different lattice constants to apply either tensile

or compressive strain to engineer epitaxial film properties, the effects of strain could be

convoluted by additional contributions from the interfacial octahedral rotation mismatch. Finally,

with the increasing use and study of ultrathin heterostructures and superlattices, where interfacial

octahedral rotation coupling could potentially play a more dominant role in controlling film

properties, such understanding is essential.

In this spirit, we use SrRuO3 as a model system to examine how interfacial octahedral

rotation mismatch contributes to the micro/macroscopic structural and physical nature of 10 nm

thick films grown on SrTiO3 substrates. In order to examine the effects of octahedral rotation

mismatch alone, we explore SrRuO3 films grown directly on bare, cubic SrTiO3 (001) and on 4

nm thick, orthorhombic GdScO3-buffered SrTiO3 (001) substrates which leverage strategies to

control lattice parameter and octahedral rotations simultaneously.29 By changing the octahedral

rotation mismatch at the SrRuO3/SrTiO3 interface with the addition of a few nanometers of

GdScO3, one can dramatically change the crystal symmetry and properties of the SrRuO3. 10 nm


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

SrRuO3/SrTiO3 (001) heterostructures exhibit monoclinic lattice symmetry with strongly

anisotropic magnetic behavior, and a Curie temperature (TC) of 148 K. In 10 nm SrRuO3/4 nm

GdScO3/SrTiO3 (001) heterostructures, the SrRuO3 lattice symmetry is transformed from

monoclinic to tetragonal and the heterostructures exhibit a higher overall film resistivity, nearly

isotropic in-plane magnetic behavior, and a lower TC = 143 K. Subsequent synchrotron-based

diffraction and half-order Bragg peak analyses reveal that although the lattice parameters are

changed, both the monoclinic and tetragonal variants of SrRuO3 have the same internal

octahedral rotation pattern (a-b+c-) albeit with a slightly smaller in-plane rotation angle in the

tetragonal variant. The observed orthorhombic octahedral rotation pattern (a-b+c-) in a tetragonal

lattice indicates a possible decoupling between lattice symmetry and internal octahedral rotation

symmetry. Such results highlight the significance of interfacial octahedral rotation mismatch and

could provide a new pathway to engineer the properties of perovskite materials.

For this work, we focused on 10 nm thick films of SrRuO3 (bulk SrRuO3 is orthorhombic

with ao = 5.567 Å, bo = 5.530 Å, co = 7.845 Å at room temperature)30 grown on SrTiO3 (001)

substrates (cubic, a = 3.905 Å26 at room temperature; henceforth referred to as non-buffered

SrTiO3) and 4 nm GdScO3-buffered (bulk GdScO3 is orthorhombic with ao = 5.745 Å, bo = 5.481

Å, co = 7.929 Å at room temperature)28 SrTiO3 (001) substrates (henceforth referred to as buffered

SrTiO3). Note that we will use cubic or pseudo-cubic indices throughout this letter unless

otherwise specified and that the subscript “O” denotes orthorhombic indices. A schematic view of

the heterostructures is provided (Figure 1b). The design algorithm is based on the fact that there is

expected to be much faster relaxation of octahedral rotation distortion at the heterointerface than

lattice mismatch strain16, 23 and thus the presence of the GdScO3-buffer layer allows for one to

produce the same lattice constants (as determined by the underlying substrate), but different

octahedral rotation patterns and magnitudes. Prior to growth, the SrTiO3 substrates were treated


<!-- Page 6 -->


6

by chemical etching and annealing following standard procedures.31 All films were grown via

pulsed-laser deposition (Methods Section). Following growth, the structure of the films was

probed via laboratory and synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction studies (Methods Section). The

electronic transport and magnetic properties were also studied (Methods Section).

X-ray diffraction studies reveal that all SrRuO3 films are fully-epitaxial and single-phase

on both the buffered- and non-buffered SrTiO3 (Supporting Information, Figure S1). Focusing

about the 002-pseudocubic diffraction condition of the SrRuO3 (Figure 1c), the SrRuO3 films

grown on buffered SrTiO3 exhibit an out-of-plane lattice parameter expansion (~0.7%) as

compared with the films grown on non-buffered SrTiO3. Rocking curve studies for films grown

on buffered and non-buffered SrTiO3 reveal that all the films are highly crystalline (the full width

at half maximum of the SrRuO3 diffraction peaks are essentially the same and are ~4-times wider

than that of the SrTiO3 substrates) and that the addition of the buffer layer does not diminish the

crystalline quality of the SrRuO3 films (inset, Figure 1c). Considering that all films are grown

with the same number of laser pulses under exactly the same growth conditions, such a lattice

expansion suggests a possible structural change of the SrRuO3 when grown on the buffered

SrTiO3. To further understand this structural change, reciprocal space mapping (RSM) studies

were completed to extract the overall symmetry and lattice parameters.

RSM studies about the 103- and 013-pseudocubic diffraction conditions of the SrRuO3

and SrTiO3 (full scans including 103- and 013-pseudocubic diffraction conditions are also

provided, Supporting Information, Figure S2) reveal that all diffraction peaks possess the same

QX values confirming that the films (both on non-buffered and buffered SrTiO3) have the same

in-plane lattice parameter as the substrate (i.e., are coherently strained) (Figures 1d and e).

Inspection of the peak positions in the QZ direction, reveals clear peak splitting for the films

grown on non-buffered SrTiO3 (Figure 1d); indicative of a monoclinic version of SrRuO3 with β


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

= 89.5°. Additional high-resolution, synchrotron-based RSMs about (Supporting Information,

Figure S3a) further confirmed the monoclinic structure and the elongated peak shape suggests the

possible existence of more than one structural variant. Inspection of the peak positions in the QZ

direction for heterostructures grown on buffered SrTiO3 (Figure 1e), however, reveals that the

103- and 013-diffraction peaks possess the same QZ values; indicating a tetragonal version of

SrRuO3. Additionally, the films grown on buffered SrTiO3 exhibit an out-of-plane lattice

expansion, consistent with the line-scans. Synchrotron-based RSM studies for the SrRuO3 on

buffered SrTiO3 were also completed (Supporting Information, Figure S3b, c). From both the

laboratory- and synchrotron-based RSM studies, the SrRuO3 diffraction peaks exhibit nearly

identical position and narrow peak shape/width along the QZ direction; consistent with a

tetragonal film. Similar to the discussion above, the observed structural change suggests that

coupling effects between different octahedral rotation patterns at the heterointerface could be

crucial in determining the film crystal symmetry. Such results call for a more comprehensive and

detailed structural analysis.

In perovskite systems, half-order Bragg peaks from X-ray diffraction are the direct result

of doubled, pseudocubic unit cells produced by internal octahedral rotations.33 Thus, synchrotron-

based half-order Bragg peak analysis can be used to extract octahedral rotation information in

ultrathin samples.34 To determine the octahedral rotation patterns (i.e., the phase relations

between adjacent octahedra), simple rules33 can be applied: 1) in-phase octahedral rotations (+)

will give rise to “even-odd-odd” half-order reflections, while out-of-phase octahedral rotations (-)

will produce “odd-odd-odd” reflections; 2) in-phase rotations giving rise to “even-odd-odd”

reflections with k ≠ l are an indication of an a+-type rotation and those with h ≠ l and h ≠ k are

indicative of b+- and c+-type rotations, respectively, and 3) out-of-phase rotations giving rise to

“odd-odd-odd” reflections with k ≠ l are an indication of a--type rotations and those with h ≠ l and


<!-- Page 8 -->


8

h ≠ k are indicative of b-- and c--type rotations, respectively. Additionally, by comparing the

measured and simulated intensities of certain half-order Bragg peaks, one is able to quantitatively

determine the rotation angles in the predetermined rotation pattern. Furthermore, due to the

orthorhombic nature of the SrRuO3 unit cell, it is possible to have four different structural

domains if the material is grown on an exact (001) cubic substrate, where the orthorhombic

[001]O is along one of the four in-plane [100] direction of the substrate.32 Those domain variants

can be thought of as rotating the SrRuO3 pseudocubic unit cell about the [001] by 0°, 90°, 180°,

and 270°, which we will denote as structural domains DX, DY, DX’, and DY’, respectively (a

schematic of these domains is provided, Supporting Information, Figure S4). Additionally, when

we complete the fittings of the intensities of the half-order Bragg peaks, we make no a priori

assumption about the make-up of the film as it pertains to these structural domains; thus, we can

also extract the volumetric ratio of the different structural domains from these analyses.

Similar analysis can be applied to the tetragonal SrRuO3 films grown on buffered SrTiO3.

First, the appearance of half-order Bragg peaks from the GdScO3-buffer layer next to those from

As noted above, comparison of the calculated peak intensities of a full range of half-order

hkl scans with the experimental data provides a route to extract the octahedral rotation angles and

structural domain fractions for the system.24, 33, 34 The fitted half-order hkl scans for the SrRuO3

films grown on both non-buffered and buffered SrTiO3 are provided (Supporting Information,

Figures S6 and S7, respectively) and the extracted rotation angles and structural domain fractions

are provided (Figure 2c). For the monoclinic variant of SrRuO3 on non-buffered SrTiO3, the

rotation angles along the three orthogonal axes are extracted to be α = 6.2° ± 1.3° (in-plane (+)

axis), β = 6.8° ± 1.4° (in-plane (-) axis), and γ = 7.4° ± 1.5° (out-of-plane (-) axis). Two majority

structural domains (DX and DX’) occupying ~70% of the volume are also observed. Therefore, the

octahedral rotation patterns can be determined to be (a+b-c-) or (b-a+c-). For comparison, in bulk

SrRuO3 the rotation pattern is (a-a-c+) with αBulk = 6.19° and βBulk = γBulk = 5.97° (calculated from

known crystal structure24, 30). Thus, in the monoclinic variant of SrRuO3, the octahedral rotation

angle in the in-plane (+) axis is similar to the bulk value, but the rotations in the two (-) axes,

especially the one along the [001] of SrTiO3, are considerably larger and the down-selection of

structural domains is consistent with prior work on growth of SrRuO3 on miscut substrates.

Similarly, for the tetragonal variant of SrRuO3 on buffered SrTiO3, the rotation angles are

extracted to be α = 5.7° ± 1.6°, β = 5.9° ± 1.9°, and γ = 7.2° ± 1.4°, which are slightly smaller

than those in the monoclinic variant of SrRuO3. Surprisingly, four structural domains (DX, DY, DX’,

and DY’) are found to occupy similar volumetric fractions in the films. Based on the discussion

above, the octahedral rotation pattern of tetragonal SrRuO3 can also be represented as (a+b-c-) or


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

(b-a+c-) (the same as the monoclinic variant). As compared to the monoclinic variant of SrRuO3,

however, in the tetragonal variant the out-of-plane (-) axis octahedral rotation remains the same,

but the two in-plane rotation angles are slightly reduced. Such a decrease in the in-plane

octahedral rotation angles results in an out-of-plane lattice expansion, while the unchanged γ

angle suggests that the octahedral rotation along the out-of-plane axis is mainly controlled by the

lattice mismatch.

What is more surprising, however, is the observation of four structural domains. The

lattice symmetry of the SrRuO3 grown on the buffered SrTiO3 is tetragonal, where the lattice

possesses four-fold symmetry about the [001] and thus only one structural variant should be

allowed (meaning one of DX, DY, DX’, or DY’ which is consistent with the lack of peak splitting in

the RSMs). Fitting of the half-order Bragg peaks, however, suggests the presence of four

different “structural” domains within the tetragonal lattice. These “structural” domains (which are

not the same structural variants DX, DY, DX’, or DY’ typically observed in SrRuO3 films grown on

cubic substrates) are the result of different octahedral rotation patterns in the films which, in turn,

give rise to a number of half-order diffraction peaks which can be fit. From the fit, we observe

four uniquely different octahedral rotation patterns where the octahedra can rotate about the [001]

by 0°, 90°, 180°, or 270°, thus giving rise to what we will refer to as “rotational” domains RX, RY,

RX’, and RY’ (Figure 3a). In other words, the combination of RSMs and half-order Bragg peak

analysis suggests that in the tetragonal variant of SrRuO3, it is possible to rotate the nature of the

octahedral rotation independently within the tetragonal lattice. The fits also reveal a nearly

equivalent volume fraction of the different rotational domains (Figure 2c). We propose that this

arises due to the presence of a number of rotational domains in the GdScO3-buffer layer. As is

common, when an orthorhombic material is grown on a cubic substrate, multiple structural

variants are formed. In this case, although the results suggest that the GdScO3 has a similar


<!-- Page 12 -->


12

octahedral rotation pattern to the SrRuO3, exact fitting of this pattern (and extraction of the exact

domain variant fractions) is difficult because of large change in the rotation pattern in the GdScO3

which is confined between non-rotated (SrTiO3) and rotated (SrRuO3) materials. In turn, we

hypothesize that the presence of various rotational domains in the GdScO3 results in uniform

epitaxial growth of the tetragonal variant of SrRuO3, but separation of the SrRuO3 in four

different rotational domains as dictated by the local octahedral rotation alignment in the GdScO3-

buffer layer which tends to drive the in-phase (+) rotation axis in the GdScO3 and SrRuO3 to be

aligned (Figure 3b).

The observation of a three-tilt (a+b-c-) octahedral rotation and the presence of four

rotational domain patterns in tetragonal SrRuO3 is not expected. Because of this we explored a

number of alternative explanations for the observed data. One potential explanation that could be

considered, is that instead of having a tetragonal variant of SrRuO3, we have an equal volumetric

fraction of four different structural domains of a monoclinic structure with an expanded out-of-

plane lattice parameter. Such a structure could potentially give rise to a similar set of RSM

diffraction patterns to that observed for a tetragonal structure. In assessing this possibility,

however, we believe that our proposed tetragonal structure is more likely for a number of reasons.

First, as noted above, the shape of the RSM diffraction peaks are consistent with a tetragonal

structure due to the lack of broadening in the QZ direction (i.e., suggesting only a single structural

variant is present) (Supporting Information, Figure S3c). Second, a highly-distorted monoclinic

structure, with lattice expansion along the out-of-plane direction, cannot be easily rationalized

considering that the strain state is unchanged and that the octahedral rotation pattern and angles

are nearly the same in the two observed structures. Third, variations in the intensity of the “even-

even-odd” half-order Bragg peaks provide an indication of the change in the monoclinic angle in

the structures. From our data (taken from samples of the same size, thickness, substrate, exposure


<!-- Page 13 -->


13

times, etc.) the intensity of the “even-even-odd” peaks from the films grown on the buffered

SrTiO3 (i.e., the suspected tetragonal variant of SrRuO3) are much lower than for films grown on

non-buffered SrTiO3 (i.e., the monoclinic variant of SrRuO3); thus suggesting that the monoclinic

angle has been reduced in the tetragonal variant (Supporting Information, Figure S6). Finally,

examination of reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) data taken during the growth

of the SrRuO3 on the buffered SrTiO3 reveals a step-flow growth mode (Supporting Information,

Figure S7). In step-flow growth, it is likely that the SrRuO3 will down-select to a single dominant

structural variant;32 suggesting that the presence of four different structural domains of a distorted

monoclinic structure is unlikely.

How, then, do we understand the unexpected observation of a three-tilt (a+b-c-) octahedral

rotation pattern and the presence of four rotational domain patterns in tetragonal SrRuO3? In the

theory proposed by Glazer18 that relates the octahedral rotation network and the lattice symmetry,

a three-tilt system is expected to have lower lattice symmetry (e.g., triclinic or orthorhombic). For

a high-symmetry lattice (e.g., tetragonal), however, it is thought that the octahedra is only

allowed to rotate along one axis (i.e., a0a0c-). Such a situation plays out in, for instance, ultrathin

SrRuO3/SrTiO3 (001) heterostructures, where it has been reported that the SrRuO3 assumes a

tetragonal structure based on the fact that certain half-order diffraction peaks are not observed,

thus suggesting only one rotation axis in the octahedra network35, 36 and others have inferred (but

not directly measured) the octahedral rotation patterns based on the lattice symmetry alone.37

Such an inference, however may not always be sound. In our measurements of tetragonal SrRuO3

grown on buffered SrTiO3, we observe the presence of a three-tilting octahedral rotation pattern

suggesting that the internal octahedral rotation pattern could be decoupled from the symmetry of

the lattice. Moreover, due to such a decoupling of the lattice symmetry and octahedral rotation

pattern, we are able to observe multiple rotational domains in a tetragonal lattice. It is important


<!-- Page 14 -->


14

to note that such decoupling is fundamentally allowed because within the calculation framework

of Glazer, the displacement of cations are not considered, and thus the symmetry given by the

octahedral network and the symmetry given by cation displacement could potentially be

considered separately.

Armed with this detailed understanding of the lattice symmetry and octahedral rotations,

we proceeded to explore how such effects could drive changes in the physical properties of

SrRuO3. The resistivity (ρ) as a function of temperature (T) was measured from 25-250 K in the

van der Pauw geometry38 (Figure 4). The high-quality of the SrRuO3 heterostructures is further

confirmed by the overall low resistivity (10-5–10-4 Ω-cm) and the relative large ratio (4-6)

between high- and low-temperature resistivity (

!!"#!

!!"! ).9 In general, it has been argued that

epitaxial strain,12 film thickness,35, 39 and stoichiometry40 can significantly affect the film

structure (i.e., Ru-O-Ru bond angle) thereby giving rise to changes in hybridization between the

Ru 4d orbitals and the O 2p orbitals which will manifest in marked changes in the macroscopic

electrical transport. From this work, however, in a situation where we have controlled film

thickness, stoichiometry, crystallinity, and strain state to be the same, variations in electrical

transport can seemingly also be induced via introduction of octahedral rotation mismatch. The

insertion of the GdScO3-buffer layer changes the lattice symmetry of SrRuO3 and also the in-

plane octahedral rotation angle, which results in an increase in TC by ~5 K and gives rise to a

large increase in the overall film resistivity (over 100% at low temperature).

We additionally studied the magnetic properties of the SrRuO3 heterostructures grown on

buffered and non-buffered SrTiO3. The magnetization-magnetic field hysteresis loops and

magnetization-temperature profiles were obtained for both heterostructure variants along two

orthogonal in-plane directions (i.e., [100] and [010]) and the out-of-plane direction (i.e., [001]).

Hysteresis loops for SrRuO3 films grown on non-buffered SrTiO3 (Figure 5a) reveal that the

SrRuO3 films have an out-of-plane easy axis that gives a saturated magnetization of ~1.46 µB/Ru

(~225 emu/cc) and projects anisotropically onto the [100] and [010]. Such in-plane magnetic

anisotropy is the result of the asymmetric monoclinic structure of the SrRuO3 which forms on the

the substrate. Additionally, a sharp magnetic phase transition was observed in the temperature-

be ~148 K (Figure 5b). Upon insertion of the GdScO3-buffer layer and transformation of the

SrRuO3 film to tetragonal symmetry, the films still exhibit an out-of-plane easy axis, but with

nearly isotropic in-plane magnetic response (Figure 5c). Also, the out-of-plane magnetization was

also found to be decreased to ~1.06 µB/Ru (~165 emu/cc). In SrRuO3, the magnetization is

strongly coupled with the orthorhombicity of the unit cell and, as has been calculated,41

increasing the unit cell symmetry from orthorhombic to cubic will lower the ground-state

magnetic moments from 1.59 µB/Ru to 1.17 µB/Ru. Thus, the smaller saturated magnetic

moments that we observed in the SrRuO3 films grown on buffered SrTiO3 are consistent with an

increase in the symmetry of the film (and consistent with the observed structural change of

SrRuO3 from a monoclinic to a tetragonal phase). Likewise, in the tetragonal variant of SrRuO3, a

reduction of the TC to ~143 K was observed (Figure 5d); consistent with the observations from

the electronic transport.

As we discussed so far, it is important to realize that the interfacial octahedral rotation

mismatch is playing an important role in determining the film structure and properties. It has been

reported that tensile-strained SrRuO3 grown on GdScO3 substrates can also exhibit a symmetry

change from monoclinic to tetragonal in the presence of a BaTiO3 buffer layer,42 which can be

qualitatively explained by octahedral rotation quenching effects where the BaTiO3 layer (with no

octahedral rotation) stabilizes the SrRuO3 into a more symmetric tetragonal phase. We have


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

repeated similar experiments with SrRuO3 grown on non-buffered and SrTiO3-buffered GdScO3

substrates and observe similar effects (results provided in the Supporting Information, Figure S8).

In the SrRuO3 films grown on compressive-strained SrTiO3 substrates, however, the structural

change from monoclinic to tetragonal upon introduction of a buffer layer with additional/larger

octahedral rotation mismatch cannot be interpreted within the same logical framework,

suggesting that one should consider lattice mismatch and octahedral rotation mismatch as a

coupled effect in determining film properties. In turn, the observed symmetry decoupling

between lattice symmetry and internal octahedral rotation network structure is likely to be a

generic feature of perovskite oxide thin films (not just an effect in SrRuO3), but the magnitude of

this effect could vary depending on the extent of hybridization of the states arising from the A-site

cation and those of the B-site and anion lattice. For instance, similar results have been reported on

SrTiO3 thin films grown on tensile substrates wherein the lattice appears to be tetragonal while

the internal octahedral rotation pattern belongs to orthorhombic symmetry group Cmcm.43

Likewise, for BiFeO3 films on (LaAlO3)0.3(Sr2AlTaO6)0.7substrates, the tetragonal lattice as

probed by synchrotron radiation contains a monoclinic, polar symmetry.44 Such findings deserve

further studies and could be potentially useful in designing novel ultrathin/superlattice perovskite

systems.

In summary, we have explored the effects of octahedral rotation mismatch at

heterointerfaces on the lattice symmetry, octahedral rotation pattern, electrical transport, and

magnetic properties of SrRuO3 thin films. Several key findings have been made. First, we have

demonstrated that for SrRuO3 films grown on non-buffered and buffered SrTiO3, even under the

same lattice mismatch, that one is able to change the film lattice symmetry and corresponding

electrical and magnetic behaviors by changing the interfacial octahedral rotation patterns.

Detailed structure analysis via half-order Bragg peak analysis has revealed that the octahedral


<!-- Page 17 -->


17

rotation pattern of SrRuO3 grown on non-buffered and buffered SrTiO3 are both (a+b-c-), while

the in-plane octahedral rotation angles are reduced in those grown on non-buffered substrates and

nearly equal fractions of “rotational” domain are observed. The observed (a+b-c-) octahedral

rotation pattern in tetragonal variants of SrRuO3 suggest that the symmetry of the octahedral

rotation network as described by Glazer can actually be decoupled from the symmetry of the

overall lattice. These results, in turn, provide new insights into novel ways of engineering

structure and physical properties of perovskite thin films, and lead to better understand the

interaction between strain, octahedral behavior and crystal symmetry in perovskite oxide thin

films.

Methods Section

Thin-Film Growth. The GdScO3-buffer layer was grown at 680°C in 7.5 mTorr of oxygen with

a laser fluence of 1.5 J/cm2 at a repetition rate of 5 Hz (a total of 140 pulses yielded 4 nm thick

films). The SrRuO3 films were grown at 680°C in 100 mTorr of oxygen with a laser fluence of

1.5 J/cm2 and a repetition rate of 5 Hz (a total of 750 pulses yielded 10 nm thick films). Following

growth, the heterostructures were cooled at 5°C/min. in a static oxygen pressure of 760 Torr.

Furthermore, to rule out the effects of varying vicinality in the SrTiO3 substrates,32 SrRuO3 films

with or without the GdScO3-buffer layer were grown on multiple pieces of the same substrate

wafer.

X-ray Diffraction Studies. Laboratory-based X-ray diffraction was completed on an X’Pert

MRD Pro equipped with a PIXcel detector (Panalytical). Synchrotron X-ray scans were

conducted at Advanced Photon Source, Argonne National Laboratory on beamline 12-ID-D using

the Pilatus 100K detector, and at Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility on beamline 14B.

Electronic Transport and Magnetic Properties. Electrical transport measurements were

completed in a Physical Properties Measurement System (PPMS, Quantum Design, Inc). During

the data acquisition, samples were cooled from 300 K to 25 K at 5 K/min. For magnetic

measurements a Magnetic Property Measurement System (MPMS, Quantum Design, Inc.) was

used. Samples were attached onto a quartz holder using GE Varnish for in-plane measurements

and were affixed in a straw with GE Varnish for out-of-plane direction measurements. In the

magnetization – magnetic field measurements, samples were cooled from room temperature to 10

K in a 1 T field and held at 10 K for data acquisition. In the magnetization – temperature

measurements, samples were first cooled from room temperature to 10 K in a 1 T field and then

warmed up at 5K/min. to room temperature during data acquisition.
